items.title: Utilizing a GPT-based exam assistant to support practice and assessment in higher education: an exploratory study on learner engagement and perceptions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Instructors increasingly use chatbots to reduce their workload and to support students with individualized learning opportunities. However, there is still limited knowledge about how students engage with chatbot-based formats for practice and assessment compared to similar human-authored formats. This study examines whether chatbot-supported instruction can achieve similar outcomes with respect to students’ engagement, perceived fairness and perceived usefulness while reducing the workload associated with creating practice and assessment activities. We developed an Exam Assistant (EA) that delivers exam-like open-ended questions, including short case studies, provides immediate feedback, and supports automated scoring with instructor review (human-in-the-loop). The EA was implemented in a real classroom setting with N = 30 undergraduate business students at a German university. Students used the EA for practice and for a graded assignment in the first course phase, while in the second course phase, these activities were delivered via conventional Moodle quizzes. This ensured alignment between practice activities and assessment across both instructional formats . Using learning analytics, chatbot interaction logs from 224 sessions with the EA, and post-assessment surveys, we conducted a descriptive, exploratory comparison of students’ engagement patterns and fairness perceptions. Results show comparably high levels of practice intensity and perceived fairness across both instructional modes. Students demonstrated greater engagement with EA than has typically been reported in prior research on educational chatbots. Nevertheless, students perceived Moodle quizzes as more suitable for future graded assessments, a difference that appears to be driven by question format rather than by fairness concerns. Overall, the findings suggest that thoughtfully chatbot-supported practice and assessment may offer a promising pathway to reduce instructors’ workload without evident disadvantages in student engagement or perceived fairness.

items.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

analysis.discussion: GenAI has not simply added one more tool to the educator's kit; it has unsettled the very hierarchies that underwrote models like Bloom's Taxonomy. By revising, inverting, or 'UnBlooming' those models, the approaches in this article argue for designs that foreground recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth as the real work of learning, especially in an age where GenAI is marketed as doing the 'thinking' for us. The future of learning is not arriving later. It is already here, unevenly distributed across classrooms, disciplines, and institutions. The educators who will shape that future are those willing to revise their most cherished frameworks, revisit their assessment practices, and keep asking questions about the kinds of thinkers, makers, and citizens we want our students to become. As we write, and as we advocate for this change, we are keenly aware that faculty at our Higher Education institutions already carry a heavy burden with teaching, researching, and public engagement. There are a finite number of hours in a day, and faculty do not have the time to stop and redesign courses almost weekly as GenAI changes and morphs. We make a point to call for change, but we know this change cannot happen overnight. It will require the dedicated commitment of administrators to find the funding and time for faculty to make these changes. Designing for recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth means little if only a subset of students and faculty have the material and institutional support to engage in that work. GenAI cannot be framed primarily as a compliance or efficiency problem because it is a fundamental change in the way teaching and learning happen. Right now, for example, many programs and professional standards have been rigidly structured to Bloom's Taxonomy, making authentic education suffer in the Age of AI (Gonsalves 2024) . Taken together, these post-AI frameworks reframe Bloom's Taxonomy not as a ladder to be climbed, but as a historical starting point-inviting educators to design learning that prioritizes metacognition, agency, and ethical judgment in a world where answers are instant but understanding is not. As Table 3 summarizes, Bloom's/Revised Bloom's, Fink's Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom's, and UnBlooms™ do not represent interchangeable models; rather, they mark a movement from hierarchical cognition, to relational learning, to AI-era inversion, and finally to recursive, judgment-centered pedagogy. Instructors and institutions must design new structures and assessment systems to account for the reality of GenAI. This does not mean being a full-on AI adopter, but it does mean that they will need to be 'AI aware' (Watkins 2024) . Ultimately, that is why we published this article: we needed to better understand how learning works in the Age of AI and build from there. In comparing selected pre-AI and post-AI pedagogical frameworks according to how they conceptualize the relationship among process, product, cognition, agency, and metacognitive reflection, we have demonstrated how learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks can be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning. Although Bloom's Taxonomy endures, we must see Bloom's as a point to begin the revision rather than an endpoint or script. If our institutions, educators, and students are to thrive in the Age of AI, we need to begin the inquiry into what pedagogy should look like with GenAI, what we are trying to accomplish, whose learning counts, who benefits, and who is left out of the future we are building. It is an ongoing conversation, one that we are privileged to be a part of, but also one we understand must move quickly into the future as our technology, institutions, and educational priorities change (hopefully) for the better.

items.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

analysis.discussion: Generative AI disclosure should not be treated as a transparent reconstruction of manuscript production. Authors may accurately report particular operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional descriptions such as language polishing, structural editing, or idea generation remain retrospective classifications whose causal significance may not be fully recoverable. The distinction between observable actions, interpreted functions, and intellectual contributions places limits on what disclosure can establish, even when authors report their practices sincerely and in considerable detail. These limits matter because provenance information can influence scholarly evaluation. The readerly distraction model developed here distinguishes justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently connected to the disclosed operation or its plausible epistemic consequences. Such monitoring may redirect attention away from a manuscript's claims, evidence, and reasoning, and under some conditions may contribute to negative perceptions of authorial competence, originality, or trustworthiness. However, attentional displacement and evaluative stigma remain analytically distinct. Their relationship is an empirical question that can be examined through comparisons of function-specific disclosures, generic disclosures, and equivalent forms of human mediation. The appropriate policy response is epistemically proportionate reporting rather than either exhaustive provenance reconstruction or the abandonment of disclosure. Methodological reporting should make consequential research operations examinable; governance reporting should identify how adopted outputs were assessed and controlled; and production-provenance disclosure should communicate relevant circumstances of composition without claiming to reconstruct every intellectual influence. Reporting requirements should correspond to the role of an operation, the risks created by reliance on its outputs, and the evidence needed to evaluate the resulting claims. Authorship, in turn, cannot rest on nominal responsibility alone. Accountable judgment requires understanding, appropriate verification, meaningful decision authority, and answerability that can be exercised when justified challenges arise. These capacities cannot be certified infallibly, nor must every contributor personally reproduce every specialized procedure in collaborative research. Nevertheless, claims about responsible authorship can be examined through role-specific explanations, relevant verification records, and substantive responses to criticism. The distinction is between responsibility merely attributed to an author and judgment that can be meaningfully questioned and defended. The central ethical task is therefore not to determine what proportion of a manuscript originated with AI, but to establish what information is necessary for evaluating its claims and who can justify the scholarly decisions embodied in them. A defensible publication policy should make consequential operations visible without allowing technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning. The objective is neither perfect transparency nor unquestioned human authority, but scholarly judgment

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Cognitive agency concerns learners’ effortful, self-directed control over reasoning with generative AI (GenAI). Building on an existing implementation-level classification of generative AI use, this review examines how cognitive work is allocated between learners and AI tools. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Scopus and Web of Science (2021–2025) yielded 93 peer-reviewed studies, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. A realist synthesis specified an a priori program theory crossing the type of work offloaded (extraneous versus germane; cognitive load theory) with processing of AI output (heuristic acceptance versus analytical scrutiny; dual-process theory), and audited the evidence on each axis under manifest coding (reported evidence only) and latent coding (adding design-based inference). Under manifest coding, 21 studies were located on both axes; all four configurations occurred, two in a single study each, and the nine Cognitive Extension studies reported peripheral uses with analytical scrutiny. Of the 93 studies, 49 reported no learner behavior toward AI output, 69 reported no learning measure independent of AI assistance, and four reported processing evidence together with such a measure. Group differences or part-sample outcomes were documented in 30 studies; one further study reported stage differences, but no learner-, task-, or assessment-level moderator showed an interpretable corpus-level association with substitution. This evidence profile identifies the process and AI-independent learning measures needed to distinguish cognitive extension from cognitive substitution. The review restates the Heterogeneous Pathways of Distributed Agency (HPDA) Model as seven testable propositions and specifies the process-tracing and AI-independent outcome designs needed to test them.

analysis.discussion: This review specifies cognitive allocation within the learner-GenAI system and audits the evidence used to examine it. All four configurations of the program theory occur among the 21 of 93 studies reporting determinate evidence on both axes. For practice, the documented Cognitive Extension cases support evaluating bounded roles for GenAI alongside learners' verification of its output. items.title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments
items.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

items.abstract_text: Abstract The application of artificial intelligence technology in education is becoming increasingly widespread, but there is no consensus yet on its impact on learners’ critical thinking. To gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between the two, this study adopted the meta-analysis structural equation modeling method and systematically integrated data from 31 empirical studies worldwide in this field. The results show that the use of artificial intelligence is not directly associated with the improvement or decline of critical thinking, but rather appears to operate through two different psychological mechanisms. On the one hand, frequent use of artificial intelligence can easily lead to technological dependence, and this tendency of dependence can harm the development of critical thinking. On the other hand, the proper use of artificial intelligence tools can stimulate learning motivation, thereby promoting the cultivation of critical thinking skills. These two opposite indirect effects coexist and nearly offset each other; the net indirect effect was not statistically significant, whereas the direct association of AI use with critical thinking remained positive and significant. Further analysis suggests that this dual effect may vary across groups: the motivational pathway appeared especially pronounced among college students, whereas the group difference in the inhibition pathway was not statistically significant. This study, from a theoretical perspective, reveals the dual paths through which artificial intelligence influences critical thinking, providing an important reference for how to effectively utilize artificial intelligence tools in educational practice and also offering new directions for future related research. However, causal interpretations are limited by the predominantly cross-sectional nature of the included studies.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence dependence and academic performance: serial mediation through attentional control and physical fitness and moderation by grade level
items.abstract_text: Objective This study examined the association between generative artificial intelligence dependence (GenAID) and academic performance (AP) among adolescents, whether attentional control (AC) and physical fitness (PF) mediated this association individually and in sequence, and whether grade level moderated these pathways. Methods Participants were 1,461 Chinese adolescents. PF was assessed using standardized fitness tests; GenAID and AC were measured by questionnaires; and standardized scores in Chinese language, mathematics, and English served as indicators of AP. Structural equation modeling and related analyses were conducted using AMOS 24.0 and SPSS 26.0. Results GenAID was negatively correlated with AC, PF, and AP ( p &lt; 0.01), whereas all other pairwise correlations were positive ( p &lt; 0.01). All direct predictive paths among the variables in the serial mediation model and the predictive paths from the interaction terms to AP were statistically significant ( p &lt; 0.01). GenAID significantly predicted lower AP through three indirect pathways: AC (95% CI [−0.067, −0.031]), PF (95% CI [−0.190, −0.003]), and AC followed by PF (95% CI [−0.009, −0.002]). Grade level significantly moderated the AC–AP and PF–AP paths: the standardized coefficients for Grade_AC_inter and Grade_PF_inter were −0.101 ( p &lt; 0.001) and −0.164 ( p &lt; 0.05), respectively. Conclusion GenAID directly predicted lower AP and also predicted lower AP indirectly through AC, PF, and AC followed by PF. The findings indicate interrelationships among GenAID, AC, PF, and AP. Grade level moderated the serial mediation model, with a weaker negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP at higher grade levels.

analysis.methods: The final sample comprised 1,461 Chinese adolescents aged 12–17 years, including 735 boys and 726 girls. Of the 2,000 questionnaires distributed, 1,638 were returned; after invalid responses were excluded, the usable-response rate among returned questionnaires was 89.19%. According to the grade-level categories specified in the Education Law of the People’s Republic of China, the sample included 361 students in Grade 7, 350 in Grade 8, 410 in Grade 10, and 340 in Grade 11. Students in Grades 9 and 12 were excluded because these graduating cohorts may differ substantially in psychological stress, emotional fluctuations, and academic pressure, thereby increasing sample heterogeneity. Participation was voluntary, and legal guardians were informed about the study and provided written informed consent. The Ethics Committee of Sichuan Normal University approved the study (2026LSTY01). Questionnaires were classified as invalid if they contained substantial item-level missingness, could not be linked to standardized academic examination scores, or could not be linked to valid PF scores. PF records were treated as invalid when indicator scores were markedly inconsistent with the participant’s actual physical condition. The inclusion criteria were adequate proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing in Chinese and written informed consent from a parent or legal guardian. The exclusion criteria were a psychological disorder, physical disability, intellectual disability, developmental impairment, sports injury, or a similar condition. GenAID was measured using the 17-item Student Generative Artificial Intelligence Dependence Questionnaire developed by Yu and Yan (2026) . The instrument comprises three dimensions: cognitive and behavioral dependence, functional dependence, and emotional dependence. Cognitive and behavioral dependence comprises six items (e.g., “When completing learning tasks, I first consider using generative AI to help me complete them”); functional dependence comprises six items (e.g., “I believe that generative AI can meet my learning needs”); and emotional dependence comprises five items (e.g., “I believe that generative AI can understand my emotions and needs”). Items are rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) on a five-point Likert scale. All items are positively keyed and summed, with higher total scores indicating greater GenAID. Cronbach’s alpha was 0.898 in the present sample. AC was measured using the Chinese version of the 21-item Attentional Control Scale revised by Yu (2017) . The instrument comprises five dimensions: inhibitory control (five items), attentional shifting (four items), task persistence (five items), attentional focusing (four items), and divided attention (three items). Items are rated on a four-point scale (1 = never, 2 = sometimes, 3 = often, and 4 = always). Seven items are positively keyed (e.g., “I can concentrate well even when music is playing in the room”), and 14 are reverse-scored (e.g., “When I am studying, I am easily distracted if someone is talking in the same room”). Item scores are summed, with higher total scores indicating better AC. Cronbach’s alpha was 0.862 in the present sample. PF was assessed in accordance with the National Student Physical Health Standard (2014 Revision) across three weighted dimensions: body morphology (15%), physiological function (15%), and physical performance (70%). The indicators were body mass index (BMI), vital capacity, the 50-m sprint, sit-and-reach, standing long jump, the 1,000-m run for boys, the 800-m run for girls, pull-ups for boys, and one-minute sit-ups for girls. The total PF score comprised a standard score and bonus points. The standard score, calculated as the weighted sum of the individual indicator scores, had a maximum of 100 points. Bonus points were awarded for eligible indicators when performance exceeded the 100-point standard, yielding a maximum total score of 120 points. Scores were classified as excellent (≥90.0), good (80.0–89.9), passing (60.0–79.9), or failing (≤59.9). AP was derived from total scores in Chinese, mathematics, and English on large-scale, standardized, in-person examinations administered by the participating schools. Because test difficulty and scoring rules varied across schools and grade levels, raw scores were converted to standardized scores. At both the junior and senior secondary levels, the maximum score for each subject was 150 points. Scores were transformed as follows: standardized score = (raw score / total possible raw score) × 100, producing AP values from 0 to 100 ( Li and Jiang, 2023 ). After obtaining approval and support from the administrators of the sampled schools, the research team distributed informed-consent forms to all eligible students who participated in the questionnaire survey. Students completed the questionnaire only after a legal guardian had signed the form. Data collection was completed within 6 months. PF data were obtained from the test records that each school submitted to the National Student Physical Health Network. School physical education teachers administered the tests and entered and reviewed the records using standardized procedures. Testing protocols, equipment specifications, and operating procedures followed the regulations of the Ministry of Education of the People’s Republic of China and the General Administration of Sport of China. Scores were classified as excellent, good, passing, or failing according to the official criteria. At the junior secondary level, PF results contributed 1 point to the physical education component of the senior high school entrance examination. At the senior secondary level, failure to meet the standard affected eligibility for high school graduation. The questionnaire was administered online, either collectively during information technology classes or outside class time under parental supervision. Completion took approximately 10 min. AP data were drawn from large-scale, standardized, in-person examinations administered by each school and were based on combined scores in Chinese, mathematics, and English. Analyses were conducted in AMOS 24.0 and SPSS 26.0. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, and overall model fit was evaluated using structural-model fit indices. Harman’s single-factor test was used to assess common method bias. Descriptive statistics summarized the study variables, and Pearson correlations quantified their bivariate associations. Path coefficients and direct effects were estimated in AMOS by maximum likelihood. Indirect effects were evaluated using a bias-corrected nonparametric percentile bootstrap proc

Six components had eigenvalues greater than 1, and the first component accounted for 26.507% of the total variance ( Figure 2 ). Because this value was below the stated 40% threshold, common method bias was within the acceptable limit ( Yu et al., 2026 ). analysis.discussion: This study tested a moderated serial mediation model. GenAID was a significant negative direct predictor of adolescents’ AP and also negatively predicted AP indirectly through AC and PF. Grade level also moderated the serial mediation model: the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP weakened as grade level increased. The correlation and prediction analyses indicated interrelationships among GenAID, AC, PF, and AP. The association between GenAID and AP is thus part of a broader pattern of relationships involving cognitive functioning and PF indicators. The findings supported H1: GenAID significantly and negatively predicted AP directly, with higher GenAID scores corresponding to lower adolescent AP. GenAID can have contrasting implications for adolescent AP. Cognitive offloading theory holds that sustained overreliance on external tools may diminish deep processing and independent thought ( Risko and Gilbert, 2016 ). Once cognitive outsourcing becomes routine, the apparent reduction in cognitive load provided by external tools becomes a maladaptive transfer of that load, compromising deep processing and disrupting the allocation of cognitive resources. Adolescents may outsource complex thinking processes, including independent thought, decision-making, and information processing, to GenAI. Although this may reduce cognitive load in the short term, the development of dependence can lead to the continued depletion and impairment of cognitive functioning. Previous research suggests that GenAI’s capacity to generate text, images, video, and audio can substantially improve adolescents’ learning efficiency ( Kasneci et al., 2023 ), whereas excessive dependence can reduce independent thinking and impair cognitive functioning ( Zhang et al., 2024 ). Academic emotions and anxiety also shape adolescent AP. Persistent dependence on AI can heighten academic anxiety, prompt doubts about one’s abilities, and reduce academic self-efficacy, adversely affecting AP ( Li et al., 2026 ). A 30-month longitudinal study of 26,811 Chinese students in Grades 7–12 across nine subjects found that AI assistance increased homework scores by approximately 18% and reduced completion time by 30%, while examination scores decreased by 18%–24%. Learning losses were concentrated among approximately 80% of AI users whose behavior was consistent with homework outsourcing, as indicated by exceptionally short homework completion times combined with high homework scores. AI users whose homework completion times were similar to those of nonusers experienced small learning losses ( Strömberg and Lei, 2026 ). These findings support the interpretation that GenAID is negatively correlated with academic performance. GenAID negatively predicted adolescent AP through AC, consistent with H2. The negative indirect estimate through AC was lower than the direct estimate for GenAID predicting AP, suggesting that stronger AC can reduce the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP. Previous research has linked excessive AI use in adolescence to neurobiological changes, including reduced prefrontal-cortex activation and lower hippocampal gray-matter density; these changes may contribute to cognitive-overload symptoms such as distractibility and impaired decision-making ( de Sousa et al., 2026 ). Excessive dependence on AI has also been associated with poorer long-term memory retention and AC ( Deckker and Sumanasekara, 2025 ). AC, in turn, is consistently associated with adolescent AP: impaired AC is related to poorer AP ( Bruce et al., 2016 ), whereas stronger AC is related to better AP ( Ma and Li, 2023 ; Song et al., 2018 ). AI’s predictive relationships with adolescent cognitive functioning and AP differ substantially according to how individuals use it. Research suggests that the learning benefits of AI depend on students’ AI literacy and how they prompt AI and verify its output. Higher AI literacy can positively predict AP through prompting practices, information verification, AI-assisted calibration accuracy, and perceived task cognitive load ( Shen, 2026 ). AI also has the potential to provide students with personalized, efficient learning experiences ( Xuan, 2025 ). In the present study, the negative indirect effect via AC was the largest, indicating that AC constitutes an important correlational pathway in the negative association between GenAID and poorer AP. The observed correlational pattern suggests that AI literacy, cognitive load and AC may co-vary with this association. A parallel pattern emerged for PF. GenAID was negatively associated with PF, whereas PF was positively associated with AP, yielding the negative indirect effect proposed in H3. The negative indirect estimate through PF was lower than the direct estimate for GenAID predicting AP, suggesting that higher PF can reduce the negative predictive relationship between GenAID and AP. Prior research suggests that excessive AI dependence among adolescents may involve substantial out-of-school time devoted to human–AI interaction, thereby increasing sedentary behavior, reducing time available for exercise, and lowering PF ( Liu et al., 2026 ). Higher PF, by contrast, has been associated with better AP ( Wen et al., 2018 ; Liang and Li, 2020 ). These findings offer a plausible account of the observed indirect effect: by displacing time otherwise available for exercise, GenAID may gradually compromise PF, with downstream implications for AP. Cognitive behavioral therapy interventions can alleviate negative emotions, stress, anxiety, and related psychological problems. Health-risk behaviors in adolescence tend to cluster, and the occurrence of one such behavior often increases the likelihood of others. These interventions can therefore target co-occurring unhealthy behaviors and psychological and behavioral problems in adolescents ( Zhang et al., 2026 ). This pattern raises the possibility that combined cognitive and exercise interventions may be associated with lower digital dependence.
